# Getting Your Time Back

> "Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil."
>
> — Ephesians 5:15–16

Ask a man why he wants to stop and he'll usually give you one of three answers: his conscience, his energy, or his wife.

He almost never mentions the plain slavery of it. Men have bled to end slavery wherever they've found it, and yet here is a man who puts the collar on himself every night and calls it his private business. The strangest part is something he never notices. On the nights when nothing stops him, he does it and wishes he were a man who didn't. The only time the habit looks precious is when he's trying to cut down, or when a week at the in-laws rules it out.

The more of the lies we clear away before you stop, the easier it will be. So in this chapter we'll look at one cost that needs no doctor, no pastor and no argument about whether it's a sin. All it needs is a clock.

## A conversation {-}

Take a young man who isn't worried. He's twenty-three and single. He sleeps fine, he feels fine, and he's read that it's harmless. Tell him it's wrecking his drive and he'll shrug. Tell him it's a sin and he'll roll his eyes. So try this instead:

"I can't believe you're not bothered about the time."

His face brightens. On this ground he thinks he can win.

"Time? It's ten minutes. It's the one small vice I've got, and it's free."

"Is it ten minutes? Count the scrolling beforehand, looking for something to get you started. Count the half hour afterwards when you lie there like a dropped coat. Count the late night and the slow morning that follows it. Call it thirty minutes a day, and you know that's generous. That's seven hours a fortnight. Every two weeks you hand over a full working day."

"Well, when you say it like that…"

"I'm not finished. Thirty minutes daily comes to about a hundred and eighty hours a year. At eight hours a day, that's roughly a month of working days. Every year. And you'll be doing it for how long? You're twenty-three. Keep it up for forty years and you've spent three and a half working years of your life on it. What did you make in that time? Who did you get to know? The woman in your head doesn't know you exist."

That last sum always lands, because he has never once thought of it as a lifetime arrangement. Now and then a man works out what a week costs him, and that's unpleasant enough. Very rarely, usually on a bad Sunday, he works out a year, and it frightens him. He never does the sum for a lifetime.

But he's in an argument now, so out it comes again: "I can afford it. It's only a few minutes." He's selling himself a set of encyclopedias on easy monthly payments.

## It was never ten minutes {-}

Be honest about where the time goes. The act is the smallest part of it.

**The hunt.** If porn is still in the picture, you know about the hunt. One coach describes it so well that it hurts: "you got 258 tabs pulled just to find a video that you like". If porn is gone, the hunt has only moved. Now it's a scroll through a feed that was supposed to be innocent, or a slow search through your own memory for a scene that still works.

**The slump.** The same man again: "One single release can take 30 minutes to an hour to feel recovery. Do that daily and it stacks into lost days, not minutes." You don't need him to tell you. You've lain there.

**The night and the morning.** A student wrote this to a Christian blog:

> "I masturbate at night so i get tired because of which i am not able to wake early in the morning."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

**The hours in your head.** These don't show on any clock. They're the minutes at your desk, in the pew and on the train when part of you is already planning tonight. Another student:

> "It makes me feel guilt and worthless, it also affected my education… as I use most of my time for masturbation instead of focusing on my studies."
>
> — another commenter on the same blog

Then add the biggest cost, which is the things that never happened. The book you didn't write. The business you talked about for five years. The language, the instrument, the friend you never rang back. The same coach says the habit leaves you "a man with a bunch of ideas, but zero execution", and every man with a drawer full of half-started projects knows what he means.

## The job offer {-}

Suppose I offered you a job tomorrow. Same work, same pay, same boss, but with one difference: an extra month off every year, fully paid, for the rest of your career.

You'd sign before I'd finished the sentence. Your only problem would be deciding where to go.

I've made that offer to plenty of men who were determined to carry on (I don't mean men like you, who are on their way out), and not one has accepted. Why not?

At this point the determined man usually says, "Look, the time doesn't really worry me." Then ask him why it doesn't. He'll cross town to save a few pounds on petrol and complain about every meeting that runs ten minutes over. Yet here he shrugs off a month a year.

Here's the reason. Every other decision in your life gets weighed. You look at what you'd gain and what it would cost, and you choose. You may choose badly, but you do choose. Whenever a man weighs this habit honestly, the scales crash down on one side, and the verdict comes back in capital letters: "STOP. YOU'RE BEING ROBBED." So he doesn't weigh it. He carries on, not because he's decided to, but because he believes he can't stop, and he keeps his eyes off the scales so that he can live with himself.

## Start dancing {-}

Now take the blinkers off for a minute.

This habit is a chain, and each link is forged by the one before it. If you don't break it, you'll be on it for life. So work out your own figure. Count what's left of your life at your own honest daily rate. For many men it comes to years.

Imagine opening your front door tomorrow and finding a parcel on the mat with all those years inside: evenings, early mornings and clear-headed afternoons, yours to spend. You'd dance down the hall. So start dancing, because that parcel is on its way.

If that sounds like a trick with numbers, you're still kidding yourself. Do the other sum instead. Work out what you'd have by now if the first time had never happened. Some men carry a very long bill:

> "I am 28 and have had this problem with lust and masturbation since I was 8 years old."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

That's twenty years, and nobody can hand them back. A young man who fought this for nineteen years said the same of his own: "I can't tell you how many years I've wasted battling with the lust". But both of them have decades still to come, and so do you.

The men who've stopped all report the same surprise, which is how much room there suddenly is. One says, "I'm saving an hour a day by getting my work done in a timely manner." Another: "I'm actually reading books again for the first time in a decade". A third took up the piano and learned to touch-type in the space the habit left behind. One man who has made a living out of telling young men what he learned gives the practical advice for all that room: pick one goal you could reach in three or four months, and pour the hours into that.

Soon you'll be making your decision. Not yet. Remember the instruction and carry on as you are until the book is finished. There's no farewell session at the end, only a prayer. Staying free after that takes one thing: you don't do it, and you don't fall for "just this once". If you're ever tempted by that phrase, remember what it costs. It doesn't cost you ten minutes. It costs you the whole parcel.

And if you're ever helping a friend out of this trap, tell him you know a man who turned down a month's extra holiday every year on full pay. When he asks who would be that daft, tell him. It's rude, but it works.

The apostle's word for what you're about to do with your time is "redeeming", which means buying back. Moses prayed about the same thing long before him: "So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom." (Psalm 90:12)

You've counted them now.
